content: Meridian Shiatsu is a specialized form of the Japanese therapy known as Shiatsu. It incorporates the Meridian theory derived from Traditional Chinese Medicine, which was historically introduced to Japan from China. Unlike Tsubo Shiatsu, which identifies acupuncture points (tsubos) based on anatomical and physiological frameworks, Meridian Shiatsu relies on the principles of meridian pathways. Despite these theoretical differences, the clinical outcomes of Tsubo Shiatsu and Meridian Shiatsu are comparable, as the locations of meridian points and tsubos are either identical or closely aligned. In 1964, a book titled Anpuku and Shiatsu Therapy, edited by Tadashi Izawa, the Vice-Principal of the Japan Shiatsu College, formally introduced Meridian Shiatsu. This work compared Anma, a therapy utilizing meridian theory, with Shiatsu therapy for the first time. Other styles of Shiatsu that integrate meridian theory were later developed by figures such as Iwajiro Sato, the author of Shiatsu Therapy and Syoatsu Therapy, and Shizuto Masunaga, the founder of Zen Shiatsu. All practitioners of Shiatsu that employ meridian theory adhere to the foundational principles established by Tadashi Izawa. Practitioners of Meridian Shiatsu engage their entire bodies in a fluid, artistic manner to facilitate transformative changes in their patients. A central tenet of this practice is the integration of diagnosis and therapy, often summarized by the mantra Diagnosis and Therapy Combined. The Japanese term Setsu Shin translates to touching diagnosis and also carries the connotation of cutting diagnosis, akin to cutting with a knife. This reflects the practitioner's ability to penetrate beyond superficial layers to connect with the vital essence within the patient. By simply placing their hands on the recipient, Meridian Shiatsu practitioners aim to induce profound transformation. The act of touching the innermost essence of the individual is considered equivalent to treatment itself. When the internal experiences of a person are acknowledged and validated by others, internal conflicts and paradoxes can be reconciled, creating the conditions for genuine healing to occur.
